title: Eyes and attention: soft focus, hard focus and the quiet eye
summary: How to switch your attention on for the few seconds of each target and off between stands, and what your eyes do: soft focus, hard focus and the quiet eye.

body.html: A round of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting takes much longer than the shooting itself. You walk, wait and watch others; the shots take only a few seconds per target. Hardly anyone can hold full attention for all that time, and you do not need to.
Soft focus while the eyes wait at the pick-up point, then hard focus on the front edge of the target.
body.heading: Watch where the eyes look

body.html: Many coaches suggest treating attention like a switch. Between stands you switch off: talk, drink water, rest your eyes. About two or three minutes before your turn, you switch on again.

When your head is tired from long, hard thinking, your aim can get worse; this has been seen in archery, for example. So adding up scores or scrolling your phone for a long time between stands may tire you more than you expect.

During the target presentation, use your attention to plan. Where does the target come from, where do you see it clearly, where will you break it? This gives you the pick-up point, the hold point and the break point: see Three points: pick-up, hold and break. When Compak® Sporting is shot by squad, only the day's first squad watches a demonstration, early in the morning (Chapter 17 · Squad: showing the targets). Later squads learn the targets by watching the shooters before them, unless a stop of more than 10 minutes brings a new demonstration of the singles.

Focus: a soft focus, calm and wide, while your eyes wait at the pick-up point; then a hard focus on the target itself, often its leading edge. Some shooters look back at the barrel or the bead (the small dot at the muzzle end of the rib) to check their lead. Lead is how far in front of the target you point the gun, and checking it this way often makes the gun slow down or stop.
The barrels stay at the edge of your vision. Experienced shooters often say they hardly notice the gun during the shot, because their eyes are on the target.

Researchers call the last steady look before a movement the quiet eye. Compared with less skilled shooters, elite trap and skeet shooters start it earlier and hold it longer, and it is longer on hits than on misses.

There is no set number of milliseconds to hold. For you it simply means: see the target early and keep your eyes on it while the gun moves smoothly. In one study, 20 skeet shooters trained this while watching video of their own eyes and shots, and they hit more targets afterwards. The research is from Olympic trap and skeet; most likely it works the same way in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

Attention is often pulled away by thoughts, not by the target: “what if I miss”, “how many have I dropped”. Worry takes attention away from the task, especially under pressure. One process goal, such as “see the front edge”, gives your attention a job: see Process goals and the score.

Attention can be trained: short rounds with a clear routine, practice with small distractions, and drills in which you follow moving things with your eyes. If your attention drifts after several rounds, that is normal tiredness; a short break helps more than forcing yourself.

key_points.html: Attention is a switch: on at the stand, off between stands.
Use the target presentation to choose the pick-up, hold and break points.
Soft focus before the call, hard focus on the target once it appears.
One process goal instead of thoughts about the score.
The quiet eye means seeing the target early and keeping your eyes on it; there is no set number of milliseconds.

did_you_know.html: Some coaches suggest a test for hard focus: try to see the rim or small details of the clay as it flies. If you can, your eyes are on the target, not on the gun.

quiz.q: How can you manage your attention during a round?

options.text: Keep full concentration the whole time
On at the stand, off between stands
Count your score after each target

quiz.explain: Hardly anyone holds full attention for long; switch it on for the seconds when it matters.

quiz.q: Where do your eyes go in hard focus?

options.text: To the bead on the rib
To the end of the barrels

quiz.explain: Your eyes stay on the target, often its leading edge; the barrels and bead stay at the edge of your vision.

quiz.q: What does research say about the quiet eye in shotgun shooters?

options.text: It starts earlier and lasts longer on hits
It must last a fixed number of milliseconds
It matters only in rifle and pistol shooting

quiz.explain: On hits the final look starts earlier and lasts longer, but there is no universal number to aim for.
